case_name: Charan Singh and Others v State of Punjab and Others
facts: The appellant-Charan Singh, a member of the Scheduled Castes, was granted 55 Kanals 15 Marlas of the land situated in the revenue estate of Katkopa in Faridkot District of Punjab State as per The policy.
In 1962, the was granted lease of uncultivable waste land and he reclaimed the land and also set up tube-well and was cultivating the land.
He found to be in unauthorized occupation of such land. Action was taken for his eviction.
Ultimately, in the impugned order it was held that since he was a lessee and the lease stood expired by efflux of time, he had no right to remain in possession thereof.

The Government had allotted the land which originally belonged to Maharaja of Faridkot; a vast extent of land was found in possession of Maharaja of which 38,000 was taken from Maharaja and 20159 kanal, 2 marlas was converted into nazool land;

Initially, the appellants had come into possession by way of a lease granted to them. They remained in possession of the land after the expiry of the lease but reclaimed the land and brought it under cultivation, obviously after incurring considerable expenses and labour.

The basic aim of the welfare State is the attainment of substantial degree of social, economic and political equalities to achieve self-expression in his work as a citizen as also Teisure and social justice.
Many a day have come and gone after 26.1.1950 but no leaf is turned in the lives of the poor and the gap between the rich and the poor is gradually widening on the brink of being unbridgeable.
The Preamble, fundamental rights and directive principles - the trinity - are the conscience of the Constitution.
issues: Whether the respondents were justified in law to take action against the appellants for their ejectment?
Whether the alienation of assigned land without permission of competent authority was held void?
petitioner_arguments: The Government had taken a decision to allot this nazool land to the members of the Scheduled Castes.
Instead, the appellant was sought to be evicted. Therefore, the action taken by the respondent-Government is not correct in law.
Economic empowerment thereby is the foundation to make equality of status, dignity of person and equal opportunity a truism.

The core of the commitment of the Constitution to the social revolution through rule of law lies in effectuation of the fundamental rights and directive principles as supplementary and complementary to each other.
respondent_arguments: The land was, though assigned for 10 years, the Government has got power to assign to the persons as per the procedure in vogue.
Pending the appeals in this Court, possession was taken and the land was auctioned to the third parties and, therefore, the appellant is not entitled to any right.
court_reasoning: The welfare State, therefore, should take positive measures to assist the community at large to act in collective responsibility towards its members to assist them.
Economic empowerment thereby is a fundamental right.
The alienation of assigned land without permission of competent authority was held void.
Economic empowerment is, therefore, a basic human right and fundamental right as part of right to life to make political democracy stable.
Justice is an attribute of human conduct and rule of law is indispensable foundation to establish socio-economic justice.
holding: The Government was not justified in taking action against the appellants for their ejectment.
The alienation of assigned land without permission of competent authority was held void.
Economic empowerment is a fundamental right.

The State, therefore, is enjoined to provide adequate means of livelihood to the poor, weaker sections of the society, the Dalits and the Tribes and distribute material resources of the community to them for common welfare.
